rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> laboratory repacked soil column experiment with two soils and six bulk densities, own air permeability measurements with a transient flow apparatus. Q2: Results, 'Impact of Aeration following Drip Irrigation on Soil Air Permeability' and Fig. 6 <U+2013> a short aeration (1050 mL for <5 min) through the subsurface drip emitter after irrigation raised air permeability within 10 min to 3.7, 2.0 and 1.5 times the pre-aeration level for the Brown Forest soil and 3.0, 2.5 and 2.0 times for the Lou soil; average post-aeration permeability about 70% (Brown Forest) and 88% (Lou) of pre-irrigation versus 54.8% and 67.6% at 24 h without aeration. Q8: Results and Conclusions <U+2013> authors note disturbed samples were used so soil structure might have been destroyed (offered to explain a contradiction with Schj<U+00F8>nning et al.) and state that further experiments with undisturbed structured soils are needed.
rows.notes: Lab column study only (two soils, three bulk densities for the aeration test, one column per treatment). Air permeability after aeration measured by a single method (modified transient apparatus); the classical-apparatus comparison was only for calibration of the baseline, so no triangulation. Mechanism (air forcing water redistribution and restoring pore continuity) is asserted as 'probably', not measured; soil water content was not measured. Effect was found to vary with texture and bulk density but no condition is stated as a requirement. No SD, SE, CI or range reported; only R2 of regressions. The claim's 'decreasing soil mechanical strength' and 'air-filled porosity' are not addressed; only air permeability is.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a laboratory soil-column experiment on aeration through a subsurface drip emitter and its effect on transient air permeability.
